4
What is the difference between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity?
A
A scalar quantity has direction but a vector quantity does not.
B
A scalar quantity has magnitude but a vector quantity does not.
C
A vector quantity has direction but a scalar quantity does not.
D
A vector quantity has magnitude but a scalar quantity does not.

hints: Look at what the four statements claim about magnitude and direction - three of them get one of those properties wrong.
Recall a pair such as distance and displacement: both can be $10 \text{ m}$, but only one needs north or east added.
Ask yourself which property is shared by both quantities and which property belongs to only one of them.
walkthrough: Recall the definitions: a scalar quantity is fully specified by magnitude only, such as mass or temperature.
Recall that a vector quantity is specified by both magnitude and direction, such as velocity or force.
So magnitude cannot be the difference, because both a scalar like $5 \text{ kg}$ and a vector like $5 \text{ N}$ have magnitude.
The difference is direction: a vector must state direction but a scalar must not.
Check the options: only the statement that a vector has direction but a scalar does not matches this rule. This is option C.

A.explanation: This reverses the definitions - scalars such as mass have no direction, while vectors such as force do.

B.explanation: Both types have magnitude - for example $5 \text{ kg}$ and $5 \text{ N}$ both state a size.

C.explanation: Both have magnitude, but only a vector also needs direction, such as velocity north versus speed.

D.explanation: Both types have magnitude - a scalar such as temperature still has a size.
